\chapter{How Are You?}
\label{ch:la-how-are-you}
\hlchaptermodality{19}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask someone in Latin how they are, and answer that I am well.}

A five-line exchange run end to end: salvē, quid agis?, valeō with grātiās tibi agō, ut valēs?, and valē from both voices.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[quid agis?]{quid agis? — how are you?}

\label{lesson:LA-C19-quid-agis}



\begin{quote}
Roman comedy gives you a short wellbeing question: \textbf{quid agis?}
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Quid agis?} literally means “What are you doing?” In the comedies of Plautus and Terence, it also works like “How are you?” or “How is it going?”

Say it in two pieces: \textbf{quid} … \textbf{agis}. Keep Latin \textbf{qu} as \emph{kw}.

That is the whole step. A second attested question comes next, after this one is comfortable.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{quid agis?}
  \item \emph{Recall:} its literal meaning — “what are you doing?”
  \item \emph{Recall:} its conversational use — “how are you?”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask “How are you?” with today’s Roman question. (\textbf{Quid agis?}) What does it say literally? (\textbf{What are you doing?})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ut valēs?]{ut valēs? — how do you fare?}

\label{lesson:LA-C19-ut-vales}



\begin{quote}
You know \textbf{quid agis?} Add one alternative built from the farewell \textbf{valē}: \textbf{ut valēs?}
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Ut valēs?} literally asks “How do you fare?” Its verb is \textbf{valēre}, “to be strong or well,” the same family as \textbf{valē}, “be well.” Plautus and Terence use this question in ordinary dialogue.

You may also meet modern \textbf{quōmodo tē habēs?} in spoken-Latin courses. It is grammatical, but it is not found in surviving classical texts. Keep that useful provenance distinction attached to the phrase.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{ut valēs?}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \textbf{valē} — “be well”
  \item \emph{Choose:} Which is classically attested: \textbf{ut valēs?} or \textbf{quōmodo tē habēs?} (\textbf{Ut valēs?})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask “How do you fare?” (\textbf{Ut valēs?}) Which familiar farewell shares its verb? (\textbf{Valē.}) Name the modern but unattested alternative. (\textbf{Quōmodo tē habēs?})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[valeō, valē]{valeō and valē — answer and farewell from one verb}

\label{lesson:LA-C19-valeo-family}



\begin{quote}
You can ask \textbf{ut valēs?}, \textquotedblleft{}how do you fare?\textquotedblright{} Its most direct answer is already hiding inside the first farewell you learned.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: valeō — I fare well}
The attested reply is \textbf{valeō}: \textquotedblleft{}I fare well\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}I am strong.\textquotedblright{} Plautus's characters can intensify it as \textbf{valeō rēctē} (\textquotedblleft{}I am properly well\textquotedblright{}) or \textbf{valeō et salvōs sum rēctē} (\textquotedblleft{}I am well and safe\textquotedblright{}).

The dictionary verb is \textbf{valēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to be strong, be well.\textquotedblright{} Watch one stem move through the exchange:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{ut valēs?} — how do you fare?
  \item \textbf{valeō} — I fare well
  \item \textbf{valē!} — be well!
\end{itemize}

That last imperative became the Chapter 1 goodbye. Latin's farewell is therefore a wish for the other person to remain well.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ut valēs?\textquotedblright{} — how do you fare?
  \item \textquotedblleft{}valeō\textquotedblright{} — I fare well
  \item \textquotedblleft{}valē\textquotedblright{} — be well; goodbye
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What verb unites \textbf{ut valēs?}, \textbf{valeō}, and \textbf{valē}? (\textbf{Valēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to be strong or well.\textquotedblright{}) Which form answers the question? (\textbf{Valeō.}) What does the farewell \textbf{valē} literally command? (\textbf{Be well.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — open, check, answer, close}

\label{lesson:LA-C19-practice}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new. You already own every word below; this lesson only puts them in order, so that for the first time you can carry a whole Latin exchange from the first breath to the last.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange — five lines, all of them already yours}
\begin{quote}
A: \textbf{Salvē! Quid agis?} \emph{Be well! What are you doing?} — \textquotedblleft{}hello, how's it going?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
B: \textbf{Valeō, grātiās tibi agō. Ut valēs?} \emph{I fare well, I give thanks to you. How do you fare?}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
A: \textbf{Valeō.} — \emph{I fare well.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
B: \textbf{Valē!} — \emph{Be well!}, the parting wish
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
A: \textbf{Valē!}
\end{quote}

Hear what holds it together. One verb, \textbf{valēre} (\textquotedblleft{}to be strong, to be well\textquotedblright{}), supplies the second question (\textbf{valēs}), both answers (\textbf{valeō}), and the farewell (\textbf{valē}). Latin does not need a separate word for \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}: the \textbf{-ō} of \emph{valeō} and \emph{agō} already is it. And the exchange opens and closes on the same wish — \emph{salvē} \textquotedblleft{}be well,\textquotedblright{} \emph{valē} \textquotedblleft{}be well\textquotedblright{} — because a Roman greeting is a wish for the other person's health, coming and going.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Run through:} both voices, aloud, once straight through
  \item \emph{Choose:} you meet a whole room, not one person $\to$ \textbf{salvēte}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the ending that already means \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} in \emph{valeō} and \emph{agō} — \textbf{-ō}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Run the exchange once more without looking. Then: which single verb supplies \emph{valēs}, \emph{valeō}, and \emph{valē}? (\textbf{Valēre}.) Which of the two Roman \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} questions is \emph{not} attested? (Neither — both \emph{quid agis?} and \emph{ut valēs?} are real; the modern one was \emph{quōmodo tē habēs?})
\end{tcolorbox}
